J. L. Austin was called a “naive empiricist” because he treated close observation—especially of how people actually use words in concrete situations—as philosophy’s basic evidence, trusting ordinary language to embody well-tested distinctions. The label is critical, suggesting that he underestimated how usage can be ambiguous or theory-laden, although Austin regarded ordinary language as philosophy’s “first word,” not its last.
